background.definition: A common autosomal dominant inherited condition characterized by heterogeneity of presentation, but typically including left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), an asymmetrically hypertrophied interventricular septum, and a potential left ventricular (LV) outflow tract (LVOT) pressure gradient.

list.listitem: Two cases per 1000 persons per year.
Two to five per 1000 persons in the general population.
One of the most commonly inherited cardiovascular disorders.
Most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.
About 40% of cases of HCM in a cohort of referred, unrelated patients were caused by mutations in at least 1 of 12 genes that encode the proteins of the cardiac sarcomere.
Inherited mutations are most commonly transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern. Sporadic mutations have also been described. C
LVH is asymmetric, with anterior septal hypertrophy being more dominant.

The hypertrophic LV is hypercontractile. The LV outflow pressure gradient may increase from 30 to 60 mm, leading to systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve. The valve may contact the interventricular septum (due to a drag effect or Venturi phenomenon), leading to subaortic obstruction (systolic murmur); this occurs in 20% of patients with HCM.
Ventricular arrhythmias may arise from "myocytes in disarray", which favors reentry.

Screen for HCM if first-degree relatives have known HCM or a history of sudden cardiac death (SCD). Clinical screening primarily with echocardiogram and 12 lead ECG, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), with or without genetic testing is recommended.
C
Primary prevention of SCD is recommended with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) in patients with HCM and prior syncope, ventricular tachycardia, or family history of SCD. B

Screening for this condition is recommended in first-degree relatives of patients with HCM, particularly in cases in which family members have suffered SCD. Few research laboratories have the expertise to screen for unknown mutations.
Clinical screening using echocardiogram, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and 12 lead ECG, with or without genetic testing is recommended.

Recommended frequency of clinical screening of asymptomatic first-degree relatives of an affected individual (Ameican College of Cardiology) is listed as below:
Age <12 years: optional unless presence of symptoms, family history of sudden cardiac death, symptoms or other clinical signs of HCM are present Age 12-21 years: every 12 to 18 months Age >21 years: every 5 years

Routine screening of all athletes for HCM during preparticipation examinations with echocardiogram, ECG is not recommended. Screening should focus on: (1) personal history of symptoms or restriction (2) family history of sudden death, Marfan syndrome, structural or arrhythmic heart disease and (3) physical exam in those aged >21: every 5 years
ECG has diagnostic value in targeting athletes for further preparticipation screening for HCM.

The presence of repolarization abnormalities (2 mm or greater inversions of T waves in at least 3 leads other than lead III) indicates increased risk of structural heart disease. Athletes with these findings should have an ECG and be monitored closely. Selective additional testing may be indicated.
In patients whose first-degree relatives have abnormal genetic testing for HCM, one may screen for HCM by performing an ECG. If abnormal, obtain an echocardiogram.
Primary prevention of SCD in patients with HCM is accomplished by an ICD in high risk individuals. B
All patients with HCM should be risk stratified for SCD.

Patients with a family history of HCM-related SCD in a close relative, multiple unexplained syncopal episodes (with or without outflow obstruction), thin-walled akinetic-dyskinetic LV apical aneurysm with regional scarring, repetitive and/or prolonged episodes of VT on ambulatory monitoring, extensive late gadolinium enhancement including end-stage progression, or massive LVH (wall thickness ≥30 mm) can be considered for primary prevention ICD placement.

In patients with preexisting disease who are at increased risk for SCD because of a positive family history for SCD or significant left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) gradients associated with HCM, the surgical implantation of ICDs to prevent ventricular arrhythmias is often performed. Long-term data to support this approach are not yet available.
All patients with prior cardiac arrest or sustained VT should have secondary prevention ICDs
HCM is diagnosed based on 2D echocardiogram or cardiac MRI showing a hypertrophied (wall thickness ≥15 mm) and nondilated LV in the absence of other cardiac and systemic disease. C
Holter monitoring recommended to detect VT.
A systolic murmur on physical examination is only present in the 20% of HCM cases with obstruction. C
ECG abnormalities are noted in 60% to 75% of individuals with HCM. C
Cardiac MRI may identify apical hypertrophy in a patient with HCM with an otherwise negative ECG.
Genetic testing can only identify 60% of the inherited cases of HCM because all genes responsible for HCM are not yet identified. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Isolated LVH without significant hypertrophy of the interventricular septum
LVH resembles HCM but because of other diseases
Some cases of HCM progress slowly to a dilated cardiomyopathy with LV dysfunction
Defects in genes of glycogen metabolism cause systemic disease and also LVH
X-linked condition; a specific form of GSC
Lysosomal storage disorder. Screen in cases of late onset (over the age of 50 y)

list.listitem: HCM is diagnosed based on echocardiography or cardiac MRI demonstrating a hypertrophied and nondilated LV with wall thickness ≥15 mm in the absence of another cardiac or systemic disease is capable of producing this magnitude of hypertrophy.
A cutoff of 13 to 14 mm can be diagnostic when associated with a family history of HCM, typical outflow obstruction or distinctly abnormal EKG patterns
A large proportion of patients remain asymptomatic.
Symptomatic patients can experience dyspnea, exercise intolerance, syncope, fatigue, chest pain of an anginal nature,or palpitations.
A positive family history of sudden cardiac death is common.
Physical examination may include a bifid carotid pulse and a loud systolic murmur (in the 20% of patients who experience subaortic obstruction).

Characteristically HCM is associated with a systolic ejection murmur that is: (1) increased in intensity with maneuvers that decrease preload such as Valsalva maneuver or standing or decreased afterload with vasodilator administration (2) decreased in intensity with maneuvers that increase increase preload such as squatting or increased afterload such as handgrip.
A systolic murmur that decreases when a patient goes from standing to squatting has a sensitivity of 95% and specificity of 85%. The LR+ value is 6.3.
A systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva has the highest specificity (96%) and highest LR+ value (16.3).
Genetic testing is not diagnostic for HCM because there is varying pathogenecity between known mutations and it is uncertain as to whether all genotypes causing HCM have been identified.
The decision to pursue genetic testing in a patient to confirm the diagnosis of HCM is reasonable.

Echocardiography is a very sensitive diagnostic test for confirming HCM and systolic anterior motion. Continuous Doppler wave examination under basal conditions of peak instantaneous left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) gradient is recommended.

Echocardiography can assess ventricular septal thickness. Using a criterion of greater than or equal to 1.5 cm, sensitivity is 90% and specificity is 43%. Using a criterion of ventricular septal thickness to posterior wall ratio greater than or equal to 1.5, sensitivity is 83% and specificity is 56%.

MRI of the heart is useful for detecting segmental LVH or for cases in which LVH is not readily apparent on echocardiodram; it is superior to echo in determining LV mass. It is also useful to quantitate LVOT obstruction after treatment with septal artery embolization.
ECG abnormalities do not correlate well (r = 0.3) with an abnormal echocardiogram that confirms HCM.
ECG is abnormal in 75% to 95% of patients with HCM.
In asymptomatic patients, treat hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obesity and other comorbidities that may contribute to cardiovascular disease. B
The first-line treatment of patients with symptomatic HCM are beta blockers, second line is verapamil, and disopyramide can be added for refractory symptoms. B
Myosin inhibitors (mavacamten, aficamten) are relatively newer agents that improve function. B
Surgical treatment with septal myectomy for HCM cases with LVOG unresponsive to medical therapy is favored over alcohol septal ablation therapy in most cases. B
Pharmacological therapy is capable of providing symptomatic relief for patients, however no change in the disease course have been observed.

Beta blockers are the first-line drugs. They have been shown to reduce LVOT gradients at rest only. Titration of dose to a HR of less than 60 to 65 in patient’s who do not experience symptom relief with a low dose is recommended.
Verapamil (200-300 mg/d), a negative inotrope, is second line therapy. Patients with bradycardia, high gradients and heart failure should be treated cautiously.
For refractory symptoms on maximum dose beta blocker or verapamil, disopyramide can be added.
Therapies to avoid include agents that cause peripheral vasodilation, increase in myocardial contractility or intravascular volume depletion.
Two randomized trials found no benefit to losartan compared to placebo.

Other calcium channel blockers are not recommended because they are vasodilators. Cardiac hemodynamic side effects such as pulmonary congestion may occur in those with substantial preexisting heart failure. Some investigators only administer verapamil to patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms and no or modest outflow obstruction.
Diuretics should generally be avoided because of the concern for excess reduction in preload, which could worsen LV outflow obstruction.

In patients with atrial fibrillation and HCM, guidelines recommend oral anticoagulation (usually with a direct oral anticoagulant) as the default treatment option independent of the CHA2DS2VASc score.

Cardiac myosin inhibitors (mavacamten and aficamten) are a new class of agents for patients with HCM and improve physiologic parameters and function. In obstructive HCM (oHCM) patients with intractable symptoms, mavacamten significantly reduced the fraction of patients meeting guideline criteria for septal reduction therapy (SRT) in a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial.

Aficamten, a cardiac myosin inhibitor, resulted in substantial reductions in LVOT gradients with most patients experiencing improvement in biomarkers and symptoms in a safety and efficacy study of patients with oHCM

A systematic review of 4 RCTs with 463 patients with HCM found that cardiac myosin inhibitors significantly increased the likelihood of a 1 category or greater improvement in NYHA class (OR 3.4, 95% CI 1.9 to 6.2).
In patients with refractory NYHA III or IV symptoms or those with provoked LVOT gradient greater than 50mm Hg, surgical therapy is indicated. B

Septal myectomy is treatment of choice. Gradient reduction postsurgery is greater than with the alcohol septal ablation (ASA) technique. Postoperative mortality is 1%. Due to postoperative atrial fibrillation, a modified intraoperative maze procedure may be done with myectomy to reduce atrial fibrillation. Mitral valve sparing procedures are preferred over mitral valve replacement due to risks of bleeding with prosthetic valve.

A novel transapical beating-heart septal myectomy (TA-BSM) procedure has been developed to simplify surgical SRT. Compared with conventional septal myectomy, TA-BSM provides realtime evaluation to guide resection while reducing surgical trauma (PMID: 37558369)

Percutaneous alcohol ablation: This is generally reserved for poor surgical candidates. A small catheter placed in the left anterior descending (LAD) septal branch is used to inject 1 to 3 mL of absolute alcohol causing a controlled myocardial infarction with associated risks. LVOT gradient reduction occurs due to reduced ejection of blood following the infarct and decreased hemodynamic force on the mitral valve, decreasing systolic anterior motion. Complications include heart block (7%), LAD dissection, massive anterior myocardial infarction, acute and late progressive mitral regurgitation, and death. Survival after ASA was similar to the background population in a cohort study of 470 patients with HCM, suggesting that this treatment is safe.

Pacemaker with DDD pacer was thought to relieve gradients among patients more than 65 years based on a randomized double blind, crossover study. However, symptom relief and exercise tolerance improvement is unpredictable. This is not recommended over myectomy or percutaneous alcohol ablation. A meta-analysis failed to find significant evidence to support routine pacing in subjects with drug-refractory symptoms.

implantable cardiac defibrillator (ICD) placement should be considered for patients with HCM who have two or more risk factors for SCD. If they have one risk factor, then decisions for ICD placement are based on case-by-case evaluation by a very experienced cardiologist who considers risks, benefits, patient's unique beliefs regarding death, participation in sports, and other factors. There is a low cardiac and non-cardiac mortality rate among HCM patients treated with an ICD.
Patients with comorbid atrial fibrillation may consider catheter ablation, although success after a single ablation is relatively low at 3 years (35%).

Recommendations for physical activity and recreational sports participation for young patients with genetic cardiovascular disease like HCM is covered in a guideline from the American Heart Association. The reader is referred to this guideline and to the Bethesda Conference recommendations, another consensus conference dealing with this topic.
Refer younger patients diagnosed with HCM for cardiology evaluation because of the risk of sudden cardiac death.

Older patients or those with a more limited phenotypic expression of HCM with no significant left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) gradient and/or LVH may be treated with a standard drug regimen. This subgroup of patients is at lower mortality risk.
Patients with complications from drug therapy or who are maximized on beta blockers may need myectomy.
Atrial fibrillation is common in HCM but there is inadequate data to inform clinical prediction tools for the development of this rhythm disorder or the likelihood of a complicating stroke.
The natural history of HCM is heterogeneous; most patients have a normal lifespan. B
Prognosis is more favorable for HCM cases with normal LVOT gradients (<15 mL/mm Hg).
Patients with elevated LVOT gradients usually develop progressive septal hypertrophy and disabling symptoms.
Wide variations in natural history have been described due to the heterogeneity of this autosomal dominant disease with incomplete penetrance.
Younger patients who present with HCM often experience progressive LVH and worsening of LVOT gradient.
Some younger patients without obstructive symptoms (and no murmur) may present with SCD.
Younger patients with obstructive symptoms need definitive medical therapy.
Elderly patients older than 75 years with HCM rarely have clinically significant congestive heart failure (CHF) and may live a normal lifespan.
Prognosis depends on the specific form of HCM.

Young patients who have had a history of SCD in their family or who, for other reasons undergo ICD placement, have an unknown long-term prognosis. The short-term prognosis with ICD placement is relatively good.
The typical patient with a LVOT gradient greater than or equal to 30 mL/mm Hg has a 1% annual mortality. More recent community-based studies have shown lower mortality rates.
Older patients with a less severe presenting form of HCM may live into their 80s and are at no increased risk of SCD.

Surgical myectomy was associated with long-term survival equal to the general population and superior survival from all-cause mortality compared to nonoperated patients with obstructed HCM. B Patients treated with either surgical myetctomy or alcohol septal ablation are at a similarly low risk of all-cause mortality or SCD.
Late gadolinium enhancement by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging for detection of myocardial fibrosis may be predictive of adverse events.
2D echocardiography to evaluate LVOT gradients is recommended. Frequency of monitoring is dictated by severity of disease and the treatment choices.
Annual 24-hour Holter monitoring has been recommended to screen for asymtomatic ventricular tachycardia in patients with HCM.

Careful observation of physical activity restrictions recommended by the Bethesda Conference and the American College of Cardiology reduces the risk of SCD in young people with a family history of SCD.
Patients over the age of 75 years comprise as much as 25% of the overall HCM cohort based on recent population studies. Echocardiography shows outflow obstruction in up to 40%.
Only a few older patients with HCM have severe CHF manifestations.

Due to incomplete penetrance of the autosomal dominant gene, the condition may not present with LVH until after the beginning of adolescence. Screening recommendations for children who have first-degree relatives with proven HCM are discussed in the Screening section.
Some investigators suggest using EKG as a screen to detect subclinical HCM in young preadolescent patients who have normal screening EKGs.

A retrospective cohort study of 128 patients with HCM presenting before the age of 19 years showed that electrocardiographic voltages, based on the sum of R and S waves in all 6 limb leads, of greater than 10 mV (P = .001) and septal thickness over the 95th percentile for age (P = .036) were independent predictors of SCD. At follow-up, patients at high risk for SCD had a combination of the sum of the R and S waves exceeding 10 mV plus septal thickness over 190% with a sensitivity of 91%, specificity of 78%, positive predictive value of 50%, and negative predictive value of 97%.
